paras: The attempted expulsion of Black residents from Orchard Park was a 1903 campaign by armed white men to drive Black families out of Orchard Park, a residence suburb of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory. It began around July 30 with a masked night visit that gave a Black household twenty-four hours to leave and turned officers away at rifle point, and on August 8 a house being built for a Black woman named Warner was dynamited. The Black residents refused to leave and armed themselves, and papers across the country reported a threatened "race war".

White residents of Orchard Park wanted "to make it a white man's district," according to a Guthrie dispatch, though Black residents already owned homes there. A later appeal by Black citizens said one of them had recently bought property in the suburb from a white owner who raised no objection to the buyer living there.

According to the Oklahoman, Wilbur Shepard, a theatre employee walking home late on a Wednesday night, saw armed men near the woolen mill on West Main Street and telephoned a deputy sheriff. The deputy, a policeman and two other men found the party at a small frame house, ordering its Black occupants to leave Orchard Park within twenty-four hours and threatening "rough usage" if they stayed. When the officers approached, they faced "a dozen winchesters" and were told to "git," and they withdrew without attempting arrests.

Estimates of the masked party ranged from about a dozen men (Shepard) to twenty-five (the policeman) and forty (the deputy). Its spokesman promised to "return again soon". Officers sent back the next night found no one, and the two Black families living in the house had not moved. Many Black residents armed themselves.

Early on August 8, a Dallas News special reported, "a mob of men and boys" dynamited and set fire to a house being built for Warner, wrecking it. The Daily Ardmoreite tied the blast to the earlier visit by "a mob of masked men". The Black residents again refused to leave, and some stocked their homes with arms and ammunition.

By August 13 the situation was described as slightly improved, and the authorities promised summary measures if needed. Black residents issued a public appeal for protection of homes bought "by the sweat of honest toil," stating that one citizen's property had been dynamited only because the owners were "simply negroes". No report of arrests, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Oklahoman's account under the headline "RACE WAR THREATENS THE CITY," detailing the masked men's demands and the officers' retreat without naming any of the party. Brief wire items on the night visit appeared in the Bryan Morning Eagle and the Barton County Democrat. The dynamiting spread further, running in the Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald ("Do Not Like the Negroes") and the Atlanta Constitution ("Whites Dynamite Negro House"). Versions also appeared in the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Richmond Times-Dispatch and the Sumter Watchman and Southron. The Bryan Morning Eagle's subhead read "Oklahoma Citizens Use Dynamite as a Means of Expulsion".

Two Black papers took up the dynamiting. The Western World blamed "a few white ruffians" from "the poor ignorant class of whites who are opposed to the prosperity of the colored people". The St. Paul Appeal remarked that the "superior" residents of Orchard Park had "shown their chivalry" by dynamiting a house being built by an "Afro-American woman".

The Oklahoman's account dates the night visit both to "about 1 o'clock Friday morning" (July 31) and to "Wednesday night or Thursday morning" (July 30). Most reports describe the dynamited house as under construction for a woman and badly wrecked, but the Western World called it a colored man's home that ruffians only "tried" to dynamite.

accounts.label: Oklahoman (via Wichita Eagle)
accounts.gist: A masked, armed party ordered Black occupants of a frame house to leave Orchard Park within 24 hours and turned officers away with winchesters; its spokesman promised to return.

accounts.label: Oklahoma City and Guthrie wires
accounts.gist: Armed men ordered Black residents, who owned homes in the suburb, to vacate; the white residents wanted a white man's district and a race riot was feared.

accounts.label: AP and Dallas News dispatches
accounts.gist: A mob of men and boys dynamited and burned a house being built for a Black woman named Warner; Black residents refused to leave and armed themselves.

accounts.label: Black residents' appeal
accounts.gist: A Black buyer had purchased Orchard Park property from a white seller; property and lives were threatened and one citizen's property dynamited solely because they were Black.

accounts.label: Western World (Black local paper)
accounts.gist: White ruffians of the 'poor ignorant class' tried to dynamite a respected colored man's home; white people denounced the act.

framing.detail: The Oklahoman's account, headed 'Race War Threatens the City' in the Wichita Eagle, reported the masked men's demands and the officers' retreat in detail and stressed the authorities' intent to prevent violence.
The dynamiting ran as a wire item across the South under headlines such as 'Whites Dynamite Negro House' and 'Do Not Like the Negroes,' framed as a feared race war.
The Western World called the dynamiters 'white ruffians' opposed to Black prosperity and appealed to 'thinking men of both races.'
The St. Paul Appeal sarcastically credited the 'superior' residents of Orchard Park with 'chivalry' for dynamiting a woman's house.

conflicts.note: The same Oklahoman account gives both; the Thursday dating is repeated with the explanation that it was after midnight.
Estimates of the first witness, the policeman and the deputy sheriff respectively.
The AP and Dallas dispatches dated Aug. 8 are the earliest and agree; the Aug. 6 dateline in a reprint is likely a misprint.

info: Night visit after midnight on Wednesday night/Thursday morning (July 30, 1903), though the same account also says 'about 1 o'clock Friday morning' (July 31).
Orchard Park, a residence suburb in the western outskirts of Oklahoma City; armed men first seen near the woolen mill on West Main Street.
Unnamed Black occupant(s) of a small frame house, said to house two Black families; the Black residents of Orchard Park generally; a Black woman named Warner whose house was being built.
No crime alleged; the stated reason was that Orchard Park was 'a white man's residence district'.
Masked, armed white men (night visit); 'a mob of men and boys' (dynamiting); described by residents as wanting a white man's district; called 'white ruffians' by the Western World.
No report that the Black residents left; the two families in the visited house had not moved by the next day.
